With the 15% bulk discount on 5+ vials of the same product, the per-vial cost drops to $76.50 — a saving of $67.50 on a five-vial order ($450 down to $382.50). KPV is also one of the four compounds in the KLOW recovery blend ($180/80mg), which combines KPV with BPC-157, TB-500, and GHK-Cu for researchers who want a pre-formulated multi-compound healing protocol.

What KPV Is and How It Works

Structure and Identity

KPV is a tripeptide: lysine, proline, valine. Formula C16H30N4O4, molecular weight about 342, CAS 67727-97-3. It matches residues 11 to 13 of alpha-MSH, the C-terminal end of the hormone. It is one of the smallest compounds we stock, which affects both how it is tested and how it should be stored.

How It Gets Into Cells

The best-known gut study, published in Gastroenterology in 2008, found that intestinal cells take KPV in through a transporter called PepT1. PepT1 normally absorbs small peptides from digested food. Once inside, KPV acted on inflammatory signalling within the cell

The Melanocortin Question

Alpha-MSH acts on a family of receptors called melanocortin receptors, including MC1R and MC3R. Whether KPV works mainly through those receptors is not settled. Some studies report weak binding. Others, including the PepT1 work, point to a route that does not need the receptor at all. The honest answer is that both may play a part.

Anti-Inflammatory Study

KPV exerts anti-inflammatory effects through two primary mechanisms studied in research: binding to melanocortin receptors (particularly MC1R and MC3R) on immune cells, and inhibiting NF-κB pathway activation — a central transcription factor in pro-inflammatory cytokine production. This dual-mechanism approach makes KPV relevant in studies examining acute and chronic inflammatory states across multiple tissue types.

KPV Research Overview

KPV research sits almost entirely in the lab. The work falls into three groups.

The largest is gut-focused. It uses cell lines grown from intestinal lining, and mouse models in which colitis is induced chemically so its signalling can be studied. The 2008 PepT1 paper is the anchor of that work. It is also the reason KPV is sometimes studied in nanoparticle carriers designed to deliver it to the gut lining.

The second group looks at skin cells and wound models, following on from alpha-MSH’s known activity in skin. The third, smaller group has looked at antimicrobial activity, which alpha-MSH and some of its fragments show in lab tests.

What is missing is human data. There are no published clinical trials of KPV, and the animal findings have not been tested in people. The mechanism is also still being worked out, as the melanocortin question above shows.

KPV has no approval from any regulator for any indication. It holds no registro sanitario with Costa Rica’s Ministerio de Salud. It is supplied here as a research material and nothing else.

How does KPV differ from BPC-157?

They are very different molecules. KPV is three residues long and is a fragment of a natural hormone, alpha-MSH. Its gut research centers on uptake through the PepT1 transporter and its effect on NF-κB signaling inside cells. BPC-157 is 15 residues long and is derived from a sequence in a gastric juice protein. Most of its research comes from one group in Zagreb, working in rats. Both are stocked here. See the BPC-157 page for its own specifications.

What is KPV used for in the lab?

It is used as a tool for studying inflammatory signaling at the smallest possible scale: which part of alpha-MSH carries its activity, how a tripeptide gets into intestinal cells through PepT1, and how it affects NF-κB. It is studied in intestinal and skin cell lines, and in mouse colitis models. It has no approved human use anywhere, and no published clinical trials.

What is the relationship between KPV and alpha-MSH?

KPV is the C-terminal tripeptide (Lys11-Pro12-Val13) of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone, a 13-residue peptide made in the pituitary and hypothalamus. Because alpha-MSH is itself the first 13 residues of ACTH, the same three residues also appear as ACTH 11-13. In lab studies, the fragment keeps a large part of alpha-MSH's activity on inflammatory signaling but lacks the part that acts on pigment cells. That makes it useful for working out which region of the hormone does what.

SLU-PP-332 is a synthetic small-molecule compound, supplied as a dry powder in a sealed 5 mg vial. It is not a peptide. It has no amino acids at all, and is a single organic molecule with the formula C18H14N2O2. We identify it correctly on this page because a surprising number of suppliers don’t.

How SLU-PP-332 Is Identified

A Small Molecule, Not a Peptide

SLU-PP-332 is often sold as a "peptide." It isn't one. Peptides are chains of amino acids. SLU-PP-332 is a small synthetic organic molecule with no amino acids in it, built from a naphthalene ring joined to a hydroxybenzoyl group through a hydrazone link. It is far smaller than any peptide in our catalog, with a molecular weight under 300 g/mol. We stock it alongside our peptides, but its chemistry and identification are different, and this page describes it as what it is.

Chemical Name, Formula and CAS Number

The chemical name is (E)-4-hydroxy-N'-(naphthalen-2-ylmethylene)benzohydrazide. The molecular formula is C18H14N2O2, for a molecular weight of about 290.3 g/mol. The CAS number is 303760-60-3. Buy AICAR: Research Grade & Lab Tested

Peptides Costa Rica supplies AICAR in 50mg vials of lyophilised powder, tested by HPLC with a Certificate of Analysis issued per batch. AICAR is not a peptide. It is a nucleoside analogue: a purine-like imidazole carboxamide base joined to a ribose sugar, containing no amino acids and no peptide bonds. It is sold under three names that all refer to the same molecule — AICAR, acadesine, and AICA riboside — and it carries an assigned international non-proprietary name, which most compounds in this catalogue do not. Because it is a small molecule, purity by HPLC applies normally and identity is confirmed against a defined molecular weight rather than a sequence.

A naming point worth stating clearly, because most vendors get it wrong. The abbreviation AICAR is commonly expanded as 5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide. That expansion describes ZMP, the monophosphate that forms inside the cell after uptake. The compound supplied in a vial is the riboside, one phosphate group lighter, with a different formula and a different CAS number. We list the riboside because that is what we ship. If a supplier’s label gives the ribonucleotide name against a molecular weight of 258.23, the name and the number disagree.

What AICAR Is and What the Studies Measured

Studies exploring Adamax have focused on its influence on cognitive performance, neuroprotection, and neurological recovery. Researchers have documented the following areas of interest:

 

Compound Class and Identity

AICAR is a nucleoside analogue, not a peptide. Its chemical name is 5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide-1-β-D-ribofuranoside; it is also called acadesine, its international non-proprietary name, and AICA riboside. CAS 2627-69-2, molecular formula C9H14N4O5, molecular weight 258.23. The ATC code C01EB13 was assigned during its clinical development. Supplied as a lyophilised powder in 50mg vials.

How It Reaches Its Target

AICAR enters cells through adenosine transporters and is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase to AICAR monophosphate, known as ZMP. ZMP is a structural mimic of AMP. It binds the gamma subunit of AMP-activated protein kinase at the nucleotide-binding sites, producing allosteric activation without a genuine change in the cell's AMP to ATP ratio. That two-step route is why the riboside, not the nucleotide, is the compound supplied.

What the Landmark Study Measured

The paper that made AICAR widely known is Narkar and colleagues, Cell, 2008, titled “AMPK and PPARδ agonists are exercise mimetics”. The model was mice. Measured endpoints included running time and distance to exhaustion on a treadmill, skeletal muscle gene expression, and mitochondrial markers. It is a mouse study. The World Anti-Doping Agency added AICAR to the Prohibited List the following year.

Clinical Development and Where It Stopped

Unlike most compounds in this catalogue, AICAR reached late-stage human trials. Acadesine was licensed by Schering-Plough from PeriCor Therapeutics and entered the RED-CABG phase 3 trial in 2009, testing prevention of reperfusion injury in coronary artery bypass graft surgery. The trial was terminated in late 2010 on an interim futility analysis. Acadesine has also been explored in haematological malignancy. It holds no approval from the FDA or the EMA.

AICAR Research Overview

AMP-activated protein kinase is a heterotrimeric enzyme that responds to the cell’s AMP to ATP ratio and, when activated, shifts metabolism from anabolic to catabolic pathways. It sits upstream of a large number of processes, which is what makes it interesting as a target and also what makes systemic activation difficult to study cleanly.

AICAR has been the standard pharmacological tool for activating AMPK in cell culture and rodent work since the 1990s, and much of what is understood about the enzyme was established using it. That tool status is the compound’s real significance. Published work spans skeletal muscle, liver, adipose tissue, cardiac ischaemia models and haematological cell lines, and the great majority of it is preclinical.

MT-II is a small, ring-shaped peptide. Six of its seven residues are linked into a loop, which makes it far more stable than the natural hormone it’s modeled on, alpha-MSH.

It was developed at the University of Arizona in the 1980s, alongside a sister compound, Melanotan I. The two went different ways. Melanotan I became afamelanotide, now an approved medicine for a rare light-sensitivity disorder. MT-II was never approved for anything, and its developer stopped work on it in 2000. A close relative, bremelanotide, was developed from it instead.

MT-II has not been approved by any regulator, anywhere, for any use. Several national medicines regulators have issued public warnings about it.

At Peptides Costa Rica it comes as a 10 mg lyophilized vial, stored refrigerated at 2–8°C and away from light, with a Certificate of Analysis for your batch. Delivery takes 2–4 business days from stock held inside Costa Rica, with no customs and no import fees.

What MT-II Is and How It Works

Structure and Identity

MT-II is a cyclic heptapeptide: Ac-Nle-cyclo[Asp-His-D-Phe-Arg-Trp-Lys]-NH2. Formula C50H69N15O9, molecular weight about 1,024, CAS 121062-08-6. The ring is formed by a lactam bridge between aspartic acid and lysine. That ring, plus the D-phenylalanine and norleucine substitutions, protects it from the enzymes that break down natural alpha-MSH within minutes.

Where It Came From

MT-II came out of a University of Arizona program in the 1980s that set out to build more stable versions of alpha-MSH. The team produced two compounds. Melanotan I is a straight-chain analog. MT-II is the smaller, cyclic one. The rights were later licensed to Palatin Technologies, which ended MT-II development in 2000.

The Receptors It Binds

MT-II is non-selective. It binds four of the five melanocortin receptors: MC1R, MC3R, MC4R and MC5R. MC1R sits mainly on pigment-producing cells in the skin. MC3R and MC4R sit mainly in the brain, especially the hypothalamus. Because it hits all of them at once, its effects in lab models are broad and hard to separate. That lack of selectivity is the main reason later research moved toward more targeted compounds

Pinealon is one of the smallest peptides we sell: just three amino acids, glutamic acid, aspartic acid and arginine.

It comes out of a research program built up over several decades in Russia, most closely linked to Vladimir Khavinson and the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology. That program developed a family of very short synthetic peptides, which it calls bioregulators. Epithalon and Cartalax, both also in our catalog, belong to the same family.

The name refers to the pineal gland, but Pinealon itself is made by chemical synthesis. The published literature describes it as a designed tripeptide, not a fragment cut from a specific natural protein. Pinealon has not been approved by any regulator, anywhere, for any use.

What Pinealon Is and How It Works

Structure and Identity

Pinealon is a linear tripeptide: Glu-Asp-Arg, often written EDR. Formula C15H26N6O8, molecular weight about 418, CAS 175175-23-2. Two of its three residues are acidic and one is basic, so it carries a net negative charge at neutral pH.

Where It Comes From

Pinealon belongs to a family of short synthetic peptides from the Khavinson program. The group's working idea is that very short peptides can reach the cell nucleus and interact directly with DNA or with proteins bound to it. That idea is specific to this research group and hasn't been widely tested elsewhere.

What the Studies Look At

Published Pinealon studies are mainly in rats, plus some cell culture work. They look at markers of oxidative stress, at cell survival under chemical stress, and at how the peptide behaves in brain tissue. Most come from the same research network, and few have been repeated by independent groups.

No Known Receptor

Unlike most peptides in our catalog, Pinealon has no known receptor. Its proposed mechanism, acting directly at the level of DNA and gene expression, remains a hypothesis rather than a mapped pathway. That's the main open question in this area of research

Pinealon Research Overview

Pinealon is a good example of how different the evidence base can be from one peptide to the next. Almost all of its published research comes from one program: the short-peptide work led by Vladimir Khavinson in St. Petersburg, which has produced hundreds of papers on synthetic bioregulator peptides since the 1970s and 1980s.

The Pinealon-specific studies are mostly in rats and cell cultures, and much of the work has been published in Russian-language journals. Independent replication outside that network is limited. There are no published clinical trials of Pinealon in the Western literature. The proposed mechanism, short peptides acting directly on DNA, hasn’t been confirmed by other groups.

That doesn’t make the research worthless. It means the evidence is early, concentrated in one group, and hasn’t been tested much elsewhere.

Section S0 covers any pharmacological substance not approved for human therapeutic use by a government health authority, and Pinealon has no such approval. Anyone subject to anti-doping testing should treat it as falling under S0 and check the current list directly.

Buy CJC‑1295 Without DAC + IPA — Research Grade & Lab Tested​

This product is a mixture of two peptides in one vial, not a single compound. CJC-1295 without DAC — also called Modified GRF (1-29) — is a 29-residue analogue of growth hormone releasing hormone: the native GHRH 1-29 backbone with four substitutions, D-alanine at position 2, glutamine at 8, alanine at 15 and leucine at 27. Molecular formula C152H252N44O42, molecular weight 3367.90, CAS 863288-34-0. Ipamorelin is an entirely separate molecule: a five-residue peptide, Aib-His-D-2-Nal-D-Phe-Lys-NH2, molecular formula C38H49N9O5, molecular weight 711.87, CAS 170851-70-4.

Because the vial holds two sequences it has no single molecular weight, and identity confirmation by mass spectrometry identifies each component separately rather than validating the vial as a whole. The meaningful specification is therefore the identity and quantity of each peptide, stated individually on the Certificate of Analysis. The combined 10mg figure on the label is a mass, not a composition. Peptides Costa Rica supplies this vial at ₡54,008 with a batch certificate, held locally, delivered inside Costa Rica in 2–4 business days.

One point of clarification, because the abbreviation causes confusion. IPA on this listing stands for Ipamorelin. It does not stand for isopropyl alcohol, and no alcohol is present in the vial. Both components are peptides, both are supplied as lyophilised powder, and neither is a solvent. We publish specifications and documentation. We do not publish reconstitution instructions, volumes or protocols

What Is in This Vial

Component One: CJC-1295 without DAC

Also called Modified GRF (1-29). A 29-residue analogue of growth hormone releasing hormone, built on the GHRH 1-29 backbone with four amino acid substitutions chosen to resist enzymatic cleavage. Molecular formula C152H252N44O42, molecular weight 3367.90, CAS 863288-34-0. It carries no albumin-binding group, which is what distinguishes it from the with-DAC form and accounts for its much shorter reported half-life.

Component Two: Ipamorelin

A pentapeptide, Aib-His-D-2-Nal-D-Phe-Lys-NH2, molecular formula C38H49N9O5, molecular weight 711.87, CAS 170851-70-4. Developed by Novo Nordisk under the code NNC 26-0161. It is a selective agonist at the ghrelin receptor, GHS-R1a. The published selectivity data is the notable part: unlike earlier secretagogues in its class it does not raise prolactin, FSH, LH, TSH, ACTH or cortisol in the reported studies.

Two Receptors, Not One

The two compounds reach the same endpoint by different routes. CJC-1295 binds the growth hormone releasing hormone receptor on anterior pituitary somatotrophs, raising intracellular cyclic AMP. Ipamorelin binds GHS-R1a, the ghrelin receptor, which signals through a different intracellular pathway. Combined stimulation of both receptor systems is a recognised subject in endocrine research, which is the reason the two are supplied together.

Clinical Development of Both

Neither compound is approved anywhere. CJC-1295 reached phase 2 under ConjuChem Biotechnologies in lipodystrophy and growth hormone deficiency; development stopped after the death of a trial participant, attributed by the attending physician to pre-existing coronary artery disease and judged unrelated, but the programme ended as a precaution. Ipamorelin reached phase 2 with Helsinn Therapeutics for postoperative ileus and was discontinued for lack of efficacy

What does IPA stand for on this product?

Ipamorelin. It is a five-residue peptide, CAS 170851-70-4, and it is the second active component in the vial. IPA on this listing does not mean isopropyl alcohol, and no alcohol is present in the product. Both components are peptides supplied as lyophilised powder.

What is in the 10mg vial?

Two synthetic peptides at a stated combined mass of 10mg. CJC-1295 without DAC, a 29-residue GHRH analogue also called Modified GRF (1-29), CAS 863288-34-0. And Ipamorelin, a pentapeptide, CAS 170851-70-4. The quantity of each is stated on the batch Certificate of Analysis rather than inferred from the combined total.

How does this differ from CJC-1295 with DAC?

The with-DAC form carries a maleimidopropionyl group on a thirtieth residue that bonds covalently to serum albumin, extending its reported half-life to roughly six to eight days. The without-DAC form has no such group; its reported half-life is around thirty minutes. They are different molecules with different CAS numbers and different molecular weights. See the CJC-1295 with DAC page.

What receptors do the two components act on?

Different ones. CJC-1295 without DAC binds the growth hormone releasing hormone receptor on anterior pituitary somatotrophs. Ipamorelin binds GHS-R1a, the ghrelin receptor. Both pathways converge on growth hormone release but through separate receptors and separate intracellular signalling.

What is notable about Ipamorelin's selectivity?

The published data. Earlier compounds in the growth hormone secretagogue class also raised prolactin, ACTH and cortisol. Ipamorelin, developed by Novo Nordisk under the code NNC 26-0161, is reported not to affect prolactin, FSH, LH, TSH, ACTH or cortisol. That selectivity is the reason it remained of research interest after its clinical programme ended.

Have either of these been tested in humans?

Both reached phase 2. CJC-1295 was trialled by ConjuChem Biotechnologies in lipodystrophy and growth hormone deficiency; the programme was discontinued after a participant died, a death attributed by the attending physician to pre-existing coronary artery disease and judged unrelated to treatment. Ipamorelin was trialled by Helsinn Therapeutics for postoperative ileus and discontinued for lack of efficacy. Neither holds approval anywhere.

Are these compounds banned in sport?

Yes, both, at all times. They fall under Section S2 of the World Anti-Doping Agency Prohibited List, covering growth hormone, its fragments and its releasing factors — CJC-1295 as a GHRH analogue, Ipamorelin as a growth hormone secretagogue. Prohibited in and out of competition, with established detection methods.

How is this vial stored and handled?

Store the sealed vial refrigerated at 2–8°C, or frozen for long-term storage. Both peptides are markedly less stable in solution than as lyophilised powder, and a reconstituted mixture should be kept refrigerated and protected from light. Avoid repeated freeze-thaw cycles. Keep vials sealed until use. Material is non-sterile.

Can you advise on dosing or preparation?

No. We supply material and documentation. We do not provide dosing guidance, administration routes or frequencies, reconstitution media or volumes, protocols or cycles, and we do not refer enquirers elsewhere for them. Questions about batch paperwork, specifications and certificates are welcome.

Research Guide

Dosing & Injection Basics

Everything you need to understand about measuring a peptide dose, choosing where and how to inject, and avoiding the most common mistakes — written in plain language for buyers new to peptides.

⚠ Please read before continuing

This guide provides general educational information only. Nothing on this page is a medical recommendation, prescription, or dosing advice for any specific individual. Peptide dosing should always be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional who knows your medical history and goals. Products sold by Peptides Costa Rica are intended for research purposes only.

What’s on this page
  1. Dosing Basics: The Core Concepts
  2. Reading an Insulin Syringe
  3. General Dosing Ranges
  4. Frequency & Timing
  5. Subcutaneous vs Intramuscular
  6. Supplies You’ll Need
  7. Best Injection Sites
  8. Injection: Step by Step
  9. After Your Injection
  10. Common Mistakes
  11. Common Questions

If you have your peptide reconstituted and you are ready for your first injection, this guide walks you through everything you need to know. We will cover how dosing actually works, how to read your syringe, where to inject, and how to do it with the least pain and the least risk.

If you have not yet reconstituted your peptide, start with our how to reconstitute peptides guide first. This page assumes you already have a properly mixed vial in your refrigerator.

Dosing Basics: The Core Concepts

Before you ever pick up a syringe, you need to understand four things about your peptide.

1. Total amount in the vial (mg)

This is printed on the label. For example, a “BPC-157 10 mg” vial contains 10 milligrams of BPC-157 in total. That total is divided across all the doses you will draw from the vial over its useful life.

2. Total water added (ml)

This is the amount of bacteriostatic water you added during reconstitution. For most products in our catalog, this is 2 ml, but it varies — see our reconstitution guide for product-specific recommendations.

3. Final concentration (mg/ml or mcg/ml)

This is how much peptide is in each millilitre of liquid in the vial. You calculate it with a simple division:

The concentration formula

Concentration = Total amount in vial ÷ Water added

Example: 10 mg BPC-157 ÷ 2 ml water = 5 mg/ml (or 5,000 mcg/ml)

4. Desired dose

This is how much peptide you actually want to deliver per injection. Research dosing ranges vary widely between peptides — covered in the next section.

Once you know all four numbers, the math to calculate your injection volume is straightforward, and so is reading it on the syringe.

Reading an Insulin Syringe

Almost all peptide injections use what is called a U-100 insulin syringe. Understanding what the markings mean will save you from a lot of confusion.

  • A standard U-100 insulin syringe holds 1 ml total and is marked with 100 units
  • 100 units = 1 ml
  • 10 units = 0.1 ml
  • 1 unit = 0.01 ml

That ratio never changes. So when someone tells you to “draw 20 units,” they really mean “draw 0.2 ml.” The units are just a more practical way to read small volumes on the tiny markings of an insulin syringe.

Converting your dose into syringe units

Once you know your concentration, the formula to convert a dose into syringe units is:

The dosing formula

Units to draw = (Desired dose ÷ Concentration per ml) × 100

If math is not your strong suit, do not worry — for every product in our catalog, the per-unit dose is listed in our reconstitution guide, so you can simply look up “each unit equals X mcg” and divide your target dose by that number.

A quick worked example

You have a BPC-157 10 mg vial reconstituted with 2 ml of BAC water (concentration: 5,000 mcg/ml). You want to dose 250 mcg.

  • 250 mcg ÷ 5,000 mcg/ml = 0.05 ml
  • 0.05 ml × 100 = 5 units on your insulin syringe

That is it. Draw to the 5-unit mark and you have 250 mcg ready to inject.

General Dosing Ranges (for Reference Only)

The table below shows the dosing ranges most commonly discussed in published research and protocol literature for peptides in our catalog. These are general informational ranges, not medical recommendations. The right dose for any individual depends on factors a healthcare professional can assess, including age, body composition, health status, and the specific goals of the protocol.

Healing & Recovery

Peptide Common Range Discussed in Research Typical Frequency
BPC-157 250–500 mcg per dose Once or twice daily
TB-4 / TB-500 2–5 mg per dose Twice weekly (loading), then weekly
BPC-157 + TB-500 Blend Varies by protocol Typically daily or every other day
Thymalin 5–10 mg per dose Daily for 5–10 days, cyclical

Metabolic & Weight Loss

Peptide Common Range Discussed in Research Typical Frequency
Retatrutide Starts very low (1–2 mg), titrated up gradually Once weekly
5-Amino-1MQ 50–150 mcg/kg of body weight Once daily
MOTS-C 5–10 mg per dose 2–3 times per week

Growth Hormone Support

Peptide Common Range Discussed in Research Typical Frequency
CJC with DAC 1–2 mg per dose Once weekly (long half-life)
Sermorelin 100–300 mcg per dose Once daily, typically before bed
Tesamorelin 1–2 mg per dose Once daily, typically before bed
Adamax Varies — newer compound, check product page Refer to research literature

Longevity, Cognitive & Specialty

Peptide Common Range Discussed in Research Typical Frequency
NAD+ Start 50 mg, titrate up to 100 mg Once daily for cycles of 8–16 weeks
SS-31 4–10 mg per dose Once daily
Selank 250–500 mcg per dose 1–2 times daily
DSIP 100–500 mcg per dose Before bed
PT-141 0.5–2 mg per dose As needed, typically before activity

The most important dosing principle

Always start at the lowest end of the range and increase gradually only if needed. Going slow gives your body time to respond, helps you identify any sensitivity early, and uses your product more economically. Aggressive dosing rarely produces better results and often produces more side effects.

Frequency & Timing

How often you inject a peptide depends mostly on its half-life — the amount of time it takes for the peptide to drop to half its concentration in your bloodstream.

Short half-life peptides

Peptides like Sermorelin, Selank, and BPC-157 have relatively short half-lives, measured in hours. They are typically dosed once or twice daily to maintain steady levels.

Long half-life peptides

Peptides like CJC-1295 with DAC and Retatrutide have been engineered to last much longer in the body — days rather than hours. These are typically dosed once weekly.

Timing considerations

  • Growth hormone-related peptides (Sermorelin, Tesamorelin, CJC) are often injected before bed because your body’s natural growth hormone release peaks during sleep, and you want the peptide to support that natural pulse rather than fight against it.
  • Healing peptides (BPC-157, TB-4) are generally not time-dependent. Consistency matters more than time of day. Pick a time that works with your routine and stick to it.
  • Metabolic peptides like Retatrutide are typically taken on the same day each week. Many users choose a day where mild nausea (a common early side effect) will not interfere with work or important plans.
  • Sleep peptides (DSIP) are taken shortly before bed.
  • NAD+ is often taken in the morning since some users report energy effects that can interfere with sleep if injected too late in the day.

Subcutaneous vs Intramuscular Injection

There are two main ways to inject a peptide. Knowing the difference matters because it changes which needle you use, where you inject, and how the peptide is absorbed.

Subcutaneous (SubQ)

Subcutaneous means “under the skin.” A SubQ injection delivers the peptide into the fatty tissue layer just beneath your skin, not into the muscle below it. This is the standard route for almost every peptide we sell.

Why SubQ is preferred for most peptides:

  • Slower, more sustained absorption — better for peptides with longer effects
  • Less painful — the fatty layer has fewer nerve endings than muscle
  • Lower risk — much less chance of hitting a blood vessel or major nerve
  • Easier to do yourself — shorter needle, gentler angle, more forgiving
  • More injection site options across the body

Intramuscular (IM)

Intramuscular means “into the muscle.” IM injections use longer needles to push past the fat layer and into the muscle tissue itself. Absorption is faster.

IM injection is rarely used for the peptides we sell. It is sometimes mentioned in research protocols for specific peptides where faster absorption is desired, but for most of our products, subcutaneous is the standard route. If you read a protocol calling for IM injection, double-check that the source is reliable and consult a healthcare professional before changing routes.

Supplies You’ll Need for Injection

Have these ready before you take the vial out of the refrigerator:

  • Insulin syringes — U-100, 29 to 31 gauge, with a 1/2 inch (12.7 mm) needle. The thinner the gauge number, the thicker the needle. 31 gauge is the thinnest and least painful. Use a fresh syringe for every injection — never reuse.
  • Alcohol swabs — 70% isopropyl prep pads. You need at least two per injection: one for the vial stopper and one for your injection site.
  • Sharps container — a puncture-resistant container for safe needle disposal. Never put used needles in regular trash. Many pharmacies in Costa Rica can provide one or accept used ones.
  • Cotton ball or gauze — for very minor bleeding after injection (rare, but useful to have).
  • A clean, well-lit workspace — a kitchen counter or desk works well. Avoid the bathroom (humidity).

Choosing the right syringe size

Insulin syringes come in three common sizes. The right one depends on how big your typical dose is:

Syringe Size Total Volume Best For
0.3 ml 30 units Very small, precise doses (under 30 units)
0.5 ml 50 units Most common, suits most peptide doses
1 ml 100 units Larger doses or full-vial draws

Smaller syringes have larger, more readable unit markings, which can be helpful when measuring small doses. For most peptide users, a 0.5 ml syringe is the right default.

Best Injection Sites for SubQ Injections

You have several good options for where to inject. Rotating between sites is important because injecting the same spot every time can cause irritation, lumps under the skin, or changes in fat tissue over time.

Abdomen (most common)

The fat pad below your belly button, at least 2 inches (5 cm) away from the navel. Consistent absorption, lots of surface area, easy to reach.

Front or outer thigh

Middle third of the thigh, on the front or outer side. Good alternative when rotating away from the abdomen.

Back of the upper arm

The fatty tricep area. Harder to reach with your own hand — you may need help or a mirror.

Love handles / flank

The fatty area above the hip, around the side of your waist. Comfortable rotation option for daily injectors.

How to rotate sites

The simplest rotation pattern is to mentally divide each injection area into a grid of 4 to 8 spots, and move to a different spot for every injection. Many users keep a simple notebook or phone note tracking the site of each injection so they don’t accidentally repeat. Avoid injecting into any spot showing bruising, redness, broken skin, scars, tattoos, or visible blood vessels.

The Injection Itself: Step by Step

Here is the full process from start to finish. Read through this once before your first injection so nothing surprises you.

1

Bring the peptide vial to room temperature

Take it out of the fridge 10 to 15 minutes before injecting. Cold peptide solution stings more when it goes in. Letting it warm up naturally on the counter makes injection significantly more comfortable.

2

Wash your hands and prepare your workspace

Wash thoroughly with soap and water for at least 20 seconds. Lay out everything you need on a clean surface: peptide vial, syringe, alcohol swabs, sharps container, cotton ball.

3

Sanitize the vial stopper

Wipe the rubber stopper on top of the peptide vial with an alcohol swab. Let it air dry for about 15 seconds — do not blow on it.

4

Draw your dose

Pull the plunger of the insulin syringe back to draw in an amount of air equal to your dose. Insert the needle through the rubber stopper, push the air in (this equalizes pressure), then flip the vial upside down and pull the plunger back slowly to your target unit mark. Tap the syringe gently to dislodge any air bubbles, push them back into the vial, and re-draw until you have a clean, accurate dose.

5

Choose your injection site and clean it

Pick a spot from the sites described above, away from your last few injection locations. Wipe the skin with a fresh alcohol swab in a circular motion outward from the center. Let it dry completely — injecting through wet alcohol stings unnecessarily.

6

Pinch a fold of skin

Pinch about an inch (2.5 cm) of skin and fat between your thumb and forefinger. This lifts the fatty tissue away from the muscle beneath, so the needle stays in the fat layer. The pinching sensation can also distract from the small prick of the needle.

7

Insert the needle

Hold the syringe like a dart. For most people with average body fat, insert the needle at a 90-degree angle (straight in) into the pinched fold. For very lean users, a 45-degree angle can help keep the needle in the fat layer rather than reaching muscle. Insert smoothly and quickly — hesitation makes it hurt more, not less.

8

Push the plunger down slowly

Inject the peptide steadily over 2 to 3 seconds. Going too fast can sting; going too slow doesn’t help. Keep the needle still while injecting.

9

Remove the needle and release the skin

Pull the needle straight out at the same angle you went in. Release the pinched skin. If there is any tiny droplet of blood, press gently with a cotton ball or gauze for 10 to 20 seconds — do not rub the area, just apply light pressure.

10

Dispose of the syringe immediately

Put the used syringe directly into the sharps container. Never recap a used needle — that is the most common cause of needle-stick injuries. Never leave a used syringe loose on a counter or in regular trash.

11

Return the vial to the refrigerator

Don’t leave the peptide vial out on the counter. Refrigerate it again right away to protect its potency. This is especially important in Costa Rica’s warm climate.

What to Expect After Your Injection

Most subcutaneous peptide injections are remarkably uncomfortable-free. Most users describe the sensation as similar to or less than a mosquito bite.

Things that are normal

  • Mild redness or a small bump at the injection site for a few hours
  • A tiny droplet of blood when you remove the needle
  • Slight stinging during the injection itself, especially in leaner areas
  • A small bruise occasionally if the needle nicked a tiny capillary

Things that warrant attention

  • Significant swelling, spreading redness, or warmth at the injection site that worsens over 24 hours
  • Itching, hives, or rash beyond the injection site
  • Difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or dizziness — these are signs of a possible allergic reaction and require immediate medical attention
  • Persistent lumps or hardened tissue at injection sites used repeatedly — usually means you need to rotate sites more aggressively

If anything seems unusual or concerning, contact a qualified healthcare professional. Trust your instincts — if something feels off, get it checked.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Injecting cold peptide

The single easiest way to make an injection hurt more than it needs to. Always let the vial warm up to room temperature first.

Not letting the alcohol dry

Injecting through wet alcohol stings unnecessarily. Let it air dry for 15 seconds before piercing the skin.

Injecting in the same spot repeatedly

Daily injections in the same area cause irritation, scarring, and changes in fat tissue. Rotate consistently.

Reusing needles

A used needle is duller and may be contaminated. Even for the same vial, the same day, the same person — always use a fresh syringe per injection.

Recapping needles after use

Most accidental needle sticks happen during recapping. Drop used needles directly into a sharps container without trying to recap.

Drawing your dose hours in advance

Pre-loading a syringe and letting it sit increases contamination risk and may degrade the peptide. Draw your dose right before injection.

Pushing too hard or too fast

Injecting too quickly causes stinging and can trap small bubbles under the skin. Steady, smooth pressure over 2–3 seconds is ideal.

Going too high on the abdomen

Avoid the area within 2 inches of your navel — the tissue there is thinner and more sensitive. Stay in the broader belly area below or to the side.

Common Questions

How much does a peptide injection hurt?

For most users, very little. A properly done subcutaneous injection with a 29 to 31 gauge insulin needle feels like a brief pinch — often less than a mosquito bite. Pain typically comes from cold solution, wet alcohol on the skin, going too fast, or repeatedly injecting the same spot. Fix those four things and most discomfort disappears.

What if I draw too much or too little?

If you accidentally drew slightly less, you can adjust by drawing a bit more from the same vial. If you drew too much, push the excess back into the vial through the same rubber stopper before injecting. Always double-check your unit mark before injecting — it’s worth the extra 5 seconds.

What if I see a bubble in my syringe?

For subcutaneous injections, tiny air bubbles in an insulin syringe are not dangerous in the way they would be for an intravenous injection. However, they do throw off your dose measurement. Tap the syringe to move bubbles to the top, then gently push them back into the vial and re-draw.

Can I inject more than one peptide at the same time?

Some peptides can be drawn into the same syringe and injected together; others should be kept separate. This depends on the specific peptides and their stability. If you are stacking peptides, do your research carefully — and when in doubt, inject them as separate injections in different sites. This is also a good question to ask a qualified healthcare professional.

What if I miss a dose?

For daily peptides, take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it’s close to your next scheduled dose, skip the missed one and resume your normal schedule. Never double up to “catch up” — that increases the risk of side effects. For weekly peptides like Retatrutide, missing a day or two is typically not a problem; just resume the regular weekly schedule.

Do I need to fast before injecting?

For most peptides, no. The exception is growth hormone-related peptides (Sermorelin, Tesamorelin, CJC) — research suggests these may work better when injected on an empty stomach, since elevated insulin and blood sugar can blunt growth hormone release. Most users inject them 2 to 3 hours after their last meal, or first thing in the morning, or right before bed.

Where can I get a sharps container in Costa Rica?

Most pharmacies (farmacias) carry small sharps containers and will often accept full ones for safe disposal. EBAIS clinics and private medical practices typically have proper disposal services as well. Avoid putting used needles in regular trash for both safety and legal reasons.

How long until I see results?

Timelines vary enormously by peptide. Healing peptides like BPC-157 may show effects within 1 to 4 weeks. Growth hormone peptides typically take 1 to 3 months. Metabolic peptides like Retatrutide may show early effects within weeks but full benefits develop over months. Stay consistent, track changes carefully, and avoid the temptation to escalate doses prematurely.

Still have questions?

We respond to every customer message personally — usually within hours. If you are about to do your first injection and want a real human to walk you through it, just reach out.

Contact Us Now

Important disclaimer: The information in this guide is general educational content only. It is not medical advice, a prescription, or a personalized dosing recommendation. Dosing ranges mentioned reflect what is commonly discussed in published research and protocol literature; they are not endorsements of those doses for any specific individual. Peptide use should always be undertaken in consultation with a qualified healthcare professional who can evaluate your medical history, current health status, and goals. Products sold by Peptides Costa Rica are intended for laboratory and research purposes only.

The compounds in this category are GLP-1 peptides, supplied as research-grade material. They are produced by peptide synthesis, arrive as a lyophilized powder in a sealed vial, and are reconstituted with bacteriostatic water before laboratory use. Vial strengths run from 5mg to 60mg, so the product page rather than this text is where to check what a given listing contains. Prices are listed per vial on each product page and updated as stock moves, so check the current figure there rather than relying on a range quoted in category copy. How This Class Is Studied

Metabolic Endpoints

Most published work on GLP-1 compounds sits in metabolic research: glucose handling, appetite signaling and body composition, measured in animal models and in clinical study populations. That is the literature this class comes from, and where a researcher looking for prior work will find the great majority of it. Endpoints outside that core are far fewer and far more scattered.

Receptor Distribution

GLP-1 receptors are not confined to the pancreas. They have been identified in the gastrointestinal tract, kidney, lung, central nervous system and heart, which is why studies in this class sometimes record measures beyond the metabolic ones. Receptor presence in a tissue indicates where a compound can bind. It does not indicate what happens once it does.

Reading the Literature

A recorded endpoint is a measurement, not a demonstrated outcome. Study population, dose, duration and controls all limit what a given result describes, and a finding in one model does not transfer to another. That matters in a class where headline results travel faster than the qualifications attached to them. Read the study design before you read the abstract.

Material and Documentation

Whether research is usable at all is decided upstream of any of this: whether the material is what the label says it is, at the purity it claims. Strengths in this class span a wide range under similar names, so label and certificate of analysis are worth checking together. Every batch stocked here is independently tested and its COA is available for the lot received.

Glutathione is three residues — glutamate, cysteine, glycine — but the first bond is a gamma linkage off the glutamate side chain rather than a standard alpha peptide bond. Two ATP-dependent enzymes build it. Glutamate-cysteine ligase joins the first two residues and is the rate-limiting step, controlled by feedback inhibition from the finished product. The free thiol on the cysteine residue is the reactive part. Two glutathione molecules oxidise to a disulfide-linked dimer, GSSG, and glutathione reductase converts them back using NADPH. Administered glutathione is rapidly broken down by gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase on cell surfaces, and whether intact molecules reach the intracellular pool in any meaningful quantity has been contested for decades. Glutathione Research Overview

Glutathione was first described more than a century ago. Frederick Gowland Hopkins isolated and named it in 1921, building on an earlier observation by de Rey-Pailhade in 1888, and its central place in cell biology has not been in question since.

It is present in most cells at millimolar concentration, higher than almost any other small-molecule thiol, and the ratio between its reduced and oxidised forms is a standard laboratory readout for redox state. Glutathione peroxidases use it to reduce peroxides; glutathione S-transferases conjugate it to electrophilic compounds, which is the first step of the mercapturic acid pathway.

Those roles are textbook biochemistry and are not disputed. What is disputed is what happens when the molecule is administered from outside rather than synthesised inside the cell.

Gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase cleaves extracellular glutathione rapidly, and the question of whether administered glutathione raises intracellular levels, or simply supplies its constituent amino acids for resynthesis, has been argued in the literature for decades without resolution.

That unresolved question underlies every claim about glutathione as an administered compound, and it is why we describe the molecule’s biochemistry rather than its reported effects here.

DAC stands for Drug Affinity Complex, and it is a chemical strategy rather than a biological one. The result is a pulse rather than a sustained elevation, because the receptor desensitizes and the pituitary's stored supply is finit

Sequence and Identity

DSIP is a nonapeptide, nine residues in the sequence Trp-Ala-Gly-Gly-Asp-Ala-Ser-Gly-Glu. CAS 62568-57-4, molecular formula C35H48N10O15, molecular weight approximately 848.8. It is unusually small and unusually hydrophilic for a neuropeptide, and it carries no disulfide bridge or terminal modification. How It Was Discovered

In 1974 Marcel Monnier and Guido Schoenenberger, working in Switzerland, perfused the cerebral venous blood of rabbits undergoing electrically induced delta-wave sleep and isolated a peptide fraction from it. The sequence was determined and the nonapeptide synthesised later in the decade. The compound's name was assigned from the conditions of that experiment, which is why it describes an effect rather than a structure.

Five decades on, the basic molecular biology remains open. No receptor for DSIP has been identified. No gene encoding it has been located. No precursor peptide has been characterised, and the tissue that synthesises it is not established. Studies on its reported effects have been contradictory, with some finding an association with slow-wave activity and others finding none.

The DSIP literature is large, old and unresolved, and much of it uses synthesised analogues rather than the native sequence — reported effects have often been stronger for the analogues than for DSIP itself, which is a detail worth checking in any citation. Found by Accident, in Blood

In 1973 Loren Pickart was comparing blood plasma from young and old donors. He put liver cells from older patients into plasma from younger ones, and the old cells started behaving like young ones. GHK binds copper(II) tightly, and the complex is what most research uses. The histidine residue does the holding. Copper is an essential trace element and a cofactor for several enzymes, including lysyl oxidase, which cross-links collagen and elastin fibres. That connection between a copper-carrying peptide and the enzymes that build connective tissue is why the molecule attracted attention in the first place.

It Declines With Age

Plasma levels of GHK are roughly 200 nanograms per millilitre at age 20 and roughly 80 by age 60. That measured decline is the single most cited fact about the compound and the reason it turns up in ageing research. It is an observation about concentration in blood. What follows from it is a question rather than an answer.

GHK-Cu has a genuine regulatory identity in cosmetics. Under the name Copper Tripeptide-1 it has been a skincare ingredient for decades, and controlled facial studies exist. Those studies are small and short, and reviewers say so. More importantly, they test a topical cream on skin. NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) is a coenzyme found in every living cell. It isn’t a peptide. It’s a small molecule made of two nucleotides joined through their phosphate groups, one carrying adenine and the other nicotinamide. It’s supplied as a lyophilized powder in a 500 mg vial.

Inside cells, NAD+ does two different jobs. First, it carries electrons. It picks them up during the breakdown of glucose and fats, becoming NADH, then hands them to the mitochondrial electron transport chain, which uses them to make ATP. Second, it’s consumed as a raw material by three families of enzymes: the sirtuins (SIRT1 to SIRT7), the PARPs, and CD38. Each of these cuts NAD+ apart as part of its own reaction. What NAD+ Is and How It Works

Structure and Identity

NAD+ is a dinucleotide: two nucleotides, one containing adenine and one containing nicotinamide, joined through their phosphates. Formula C21H27N7O14P2, molecular weight about 663, CAS 53-84-9. It contains no amino acids and no peptide bonds.

Electron Carrier

NAD+ accepts electrons during glycolysis and the Krebs cycle and becomes NADH. NADH then passes those electrons to complex I of the mitochondrial electron transport chain, which uses them to make ATP.

Sirtuin Substrate

Sirtuins are enzymes that remove acetyl groups from other proteins. They can't work without NAD+: each reaction consumes one molecule of it. That dependence links sirtuin activity directly to how much NAD+ is available in the cell.

PARPs and CD38

PARPs, especially PARP-1, detect breaks in DNA and use NAD+ to build chains of ADP-ribose that mark the damage for repair. CD38, an enzyme on the surface of many cells, breaks down NAD+ as part of calcium signaling.

Most of what we stock is a peptide: a chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. NAD+ isn’t. It’s built from two nucleotides, the same kind of building blocks that make up DNA and RNA, joined through a pair of phosphate groups. It contains no amino acids at all.

NAD+ Research Overview

NAD+ has one of the longest research histories of anything in our catalog. Arthur Harden and William John Young first identified it in 1906 as a heat-stable factor needed for yeast fermentation, which they called cozymase. Hans von Euler-Chelpin worked out much of its structure, and he and Harden shared the 1929 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In the 1930s, Otto Warburg showed how it carries hydrogen in metabolic reactions.

Since the 2000s, research has shifted toward NAD+ as a substrate rather than just a carrier. That’s because of the sirtuins and PARPs, and the finding in animal studies that NAD+ levels in many tissues fall with age. That work is mainly in cell culture and rodents. Small human studies have measured NAD+ levels and how precursors like NMN and nicotinamide riboside change them. The field is active, and its conclusions are still being tested.

What is NAD+

NAD+ is nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, a coenzyme found in every living cell. It's a small molecule, formula C21H27N7O14P2, molecular weight about 663. How is NAD+ related to NMN?

NMN, nicotinamide mononucleotide, is one step before NAD+ in the cell's salvage pathway. An enzyme called NMNAT joins NMN to an adenine nucleotide to make NAD+. So NMN is a precursor and NAD+ is the finished coenzyme. Research comparing the two asks how each gets into cells and tissues, and how efficiently NMN is converted. Outside the cell, NAD+ itself is broken down fairly quickly, and whether it crosses cell membranes intact is still debated.

How is NAD+ different from Glutathione?

They're chemically unrelated. NAD+ is a dinucleotide coenzyme that carries electrons and serves as a raw material for sirtuin, PARP and CD38 enzymes. Glutathione is a three-residue peptide, glutamate, cysteine and glycine, that acts as the cell's main reducing agent, using its sulfur group to neutralize reactive oxygen species. Both are stocked here. See the Glutathione page for its own specifications.

What is NAD+ used for in the lab?"

It's used in research on cellular energy metabolism, as the main electron carrier feeding the mitochondria, and on the enzymes that consume it: sirtuins, PARPs and CD38. A large part of current work asks why NAD+ levels fall with age in animal tissues, and what consumes it. It's also a standard reagent in biochemistry labs, where many enzyme assays use it.

What is the difference between NAD+ and NADH?

NAD+ and NADH are the oxidized and reduced forms of the same molecule. NAD+ accepts electrons during glycolysis and the Krebs cycle and becomes NADH. NADH passes those electrons to the mitochondrial electron transport chain, driving ATP production, and turns back into NAD+. The NAD+/NADH ratio is a standard measure of a cell's redox state. The oxidized form, NAD+, is the one sirtuins, PARPs and CD38 use as a substrate.

IGF-1 LR3 is a modified version of a hormone the body already makes. Native insulin-like growth factor 1 is 70 amino acids and about 7,649 daltons. The LR3 version is 83 amino acids and about 9,111 daltons, and the difference is two deliberate changes.

The first is a single substitution: arginine replaces glutamic acid at position 3. That one swap sharply reduces how tightly the molecule is held by the IGF binding proteins that normally sequester circulating IGF-1, so far more of it stays unbound. The second is a 13-residue extension on the front end, carried over from how the protein is expressed. Together they are the reason the LR3 form behaves so differently from native IGF-1 in culture, and the reason it has a name of its own.

Its original and still-legitimate commercial use is as a cell culture supplement in biopharmaceutical manufacturing, where it raises recombinant protein yields in mammalian cell lines. It is a laboratory reagent by design.

What IGF-1 LR3 Is and How It Works

Structure and Identity

IGF-1 LR3 is an 83-residue single-chain protein, molecular weight about 9,111, CAS 946870-92-4. Native IGF-1 is 70 residues at 7,649. The extra 13 residues sit at the N-terminus, and position 3 carries arginine where native IGF-1 carries glutamic acid. Produced recombinantly, not by chemical synthesis.

Why the Arg3 Substitution Matters

Circulating IGF-1 is almost entirely bound to IGF binding proteins, mainly IGFBP-3, which control how much is free at any moment. The arginine at position 3 lowers affinity for those binding proteins by a large margin. The practical result is a much longer functional half-life in culture.

The Receptor It Binds

IGF-1 LR3 binds IGF-1R, the type 1 insulin-like growth factor receptor. IGF-1R is a receptor tyrosine kinase and a close structural relative of the insulin receptor, which is why IGF-1 and its analogues show some cross-reactivity with insulin signaling at higher concentrations.

What Happens Downstream

Receptor binding triggers autophosphorylation and recruits IRS-1, which branches into two well-mapped pathways: PI3K to Akt to mTOR, and Ras to MAPK. These are among the most studied signalling cascades in cell biology, which is a large part of why this molecule is used in the lab.

What HCG Is and How It Works

Structure and Origin

HCG is made of two different protein chains locked together. The alpha chain is 92 amino acids and is shared with three other hormones. The beta chain is 145 amino acids and is unique to HCG. Sugar chains cover both, taking the whole molecule to roughly 36.7 kilodaltons. CAS number 9002-61-3.

Where It Comes From

In the body, HCG is produced by the syncytiotrophoblast, the outer cell layer of the placenta, which is why it appears in the urine of pregnant women. Selmar Aschheim and Bernhard Zondek identified it there in 1927. Commercial material is either purified from that urine or made recombinantly in cell culture.

The Receptor It Binds

HCG binds the LH/hCG receptor, written LHCGR, a G protein-coupled receptor sitting on Leydig cells in the testis and theca and granulosa cells in the ovary. Luteinising hormone binds the same receptor. The two molecules overlap closely enough that HCG activates it in place of LH.

What Happens Downstream

Receptor activation switches on adenylyl cyclase, raising cyclic AMP inside the cell and switching on protein kinase A. That in turn increases StAR protein, which moves cholesterol into the mitochondria — the rate-limiting step in steroid synthesis. HCG's sugar coat gives it a much longer circulating half-life than LH.

HCG is unusual in this catalogue because it is not an experimental compound. It is an approved medicine with decades of clinical data behind it, sold in the United States as Pregnyl and Novarel and in a recombinant version as Ovidrel, and in Europe as Pregnyl and Ovitrelle. Approved indications are narrow and specific: undescended testicles in prepubertal boys where there is no anatomical blockage, selected cases of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in men, and ovulation induction in women who are not ovulating for reasons other than ovarian failure.

What Adamax Is, and What the Research Record Shows

Studies exploring Adamax have focused on its influence on cognitive performance, neuroprotection, and neurological recovery. Researchers have documented the following areas of interest:

 

Structure and Identity

Adamax is a modified analogue of Semax, a heptapeptide corresponding to the ACTH(4–7) fragment extended by Pro-Gly-Pro. Semax has a settled identity: CAS 80714-61-0, formula C37H51N9O10S, molecular weight 813.93. Adamax does not. Two different structures are sold under the name internationally, and no CAS number has been assigned to either. The identity that applies is the one on the batch certificate.

Origin and Development

The backbone comes from Soviet and Russian peptide chemistry. Short ACTH fragments were investigated through the 1980s as non-corticotropic analogues, and Semax was first described in the literature in 1991. It was later registered as a medicine in Russia and added to the Russian List of Vital and Essential Medicines in December 2011. Adamax post-dates that work entirely.

Pathway Described in the Literature

Published pathway work on Semax concerns transcription and neurotrophic signalling in rodent brain tissue: altered expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor and its receptor TrkB, changes in nerve growth factor expression, and modulation of monoaminergic transmission. Semax lacks the melanocortin receptor binding profile of full-length ACTH, which is why the fragment was selected. All of this describes Semax.

Strength of the Evidence

The Semax literature is substantial but largely Russian-language, with limited independent replication outside Russia and few large randomised controlled trials. For Adamax specifically there is no peer-reviewed primary literature, no pharmacokinetic data, and no published potency comparison. Figures circulating in the trade — fold-potency multiples, half-life ranges — trace to vendor copy rather than to a citable study.

Adamax Research Overview

Built as an synthetic modification of Semax, Adamax is a Russian nootropic peptide with three decades of clinical history. It comes from the family of ACTH(4–10)-derived cognitive peptides. The primary reason why it was created was to solve a specific problem with its parent compound: Semax clears from the body extremely fast.

The approach is a familiar one in drug design — take a molecule that works and chemically armour it so it lasts longer and reaches the brain more readily. That’s the entire premise of Adamax. Whether it succeeds is a separate question, and one researchers are trying to find out consistently.

No toxicology package has been published for Adamax. There are no LD50 data, no repeat-dose toxicity studies and no genotoxicity screening for this compound. Absence of reported harm here means absence of testing, not absence of risk. Handle as an uncharacterised research chemical: lyophilised peptide powder is hygroscopic and readily aerosolised, so weigh in a controlled environment with appropriate protective equipment. It is a single synthetic peptide: the full 44-amino-acid sequence of human growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), with a trans-3-hexenoyl group attached to the first amino acid. How Tesamorelin Is Identified

Sequence

Tesamorelin is a chain of 44 amino acids: YADAIFTNSYRKVLGQLSARKLLQDIMSRQQGESNQERGARARL-NH2. This is the full sequence of human GHRH, ending in an amide group.

TB-500

TB-500 is a synthetic peptide modeled on the actin-binding region of thymosin beta-4, a 43-residue protein found in almost every cell. Thymosin beta-4's main known job is holding G-actin, the single-unit form of the protein that builds the cell's internal skeleton. How closely the short fragment reproduces the full protein's activity is not well established.

GHK-Cu

GHK-Cu is the tripeptide glycyl-histidyl-lysine bound to a copper(II) ion. Loren Pickart isolated it from human plasma in 1973. The peptide binds copper tightly and carries it into cells. KPV is the tripeptide lysine-proline-valine, the last three residues of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone. It keeps some of the parent hormone's activity on inflammatory signaling but lacks the part that acts on pigment cells. Research is preclinical — cell lines and rodent colitis models — and it has been studied for its effects on the NF-κB pathway. Molecular weight about 342.

Buy MOTS-C in Costa Rica: Research Grade & Lab Tested

Most of the peptides in our catalog are copies of, or variations on, sequences written in the cell’s nuclear DNA. MOTS-c is different. Its sequence sits inside the small, separate genome carried by mitochondria, in the gene for a piece of ribosomal RNA called 12S. That’s where its name comes from: Mitochondrial Open reading frame of the Twelve S rRNA, type c.

It was identified in 2015 by Changhan Lee and colleagues at the University of Southern California. It joined a small family of signaling peptides encoded by mitochondria, alongside humanin.

The MOTS-c we sell is made by chemical synthesis, not extracted from cells. It’s a synthetic peptide with the same 16-residue sequence. MOTS-c has not been approved by any regulator, anywhere, for any use.

It comes in two sizes, 10 mg and 40 mg, as lyophilized powder, stored refrigerated at 2–8°C, with a Certificate of Analysis for your batch. Five or more vials of the same size get an automatic 15% discount. Delivery takes 2–4 business days from stock held inside Costa Rica, with no customs and no import fees.

What MOTS-c Is and How It Works

Structure and Origin

MOTS-c is 16 amino acids long: Met-Arg-Trp-Gln-Glu-Met-Gly-Tyr-Ile-Phe-Tyr-Pro-Arg-Lys-Leu-Arg. Formula C101H152N28O22S2, molecular weight about 2,175, CAS 1627580-64-6. Its natural sequence is encoded in the mitochondrial 12S rRNA gene, making it one of a small family of mitochondrial-derived peptides. The version in our vials is chemically synthesized to match it.

The AMPK Connection

In cell and mouse studies, MOTS-c activates AMPK, an enzyme that acts as a cell's energy sensor. The original 2015 work traced this to an effect on the folate cycle, which raises levels of AICAR, a natural molecule that switches AMPK on. 191 amino acids in a single chain, with two internal disulfide bridges, folded into a four-helix bundle. Molecular weight about 22,124. Recombinant DNA technology. The human growth hormone gene is expressed in cultured cells — historically E. coli, also mammalian lines — and the protein is purified from the culture. The generic HGH vials (12 IU, 24 IU, 30 IU) are research-grade recombinant human growth hormone (rHGH, Somatropin) manufactured to high purity standards and supplied with a Certificate of Analysis. The Pfizer Genotropin 50 IU is a pharmaceutical-brand product manufactured by Pfizer under regulated pharmaceutical production standards — the same Somatropin molecule, but produced within a licensed pharmaceutical supply chain. The Pfizer brand is typically chosen when pharmaceutical-grade provenance documentation is a requirement for the research protocol. It is priced at $5.50/IU versus $4.17/IU for the generic 30 IU, reflecting the brand premium.

What are the Common Research Applications of HGH Peptides?

HGH peptides primarily serve research purposes in exploring the mechanisms of growth hormone production and its effects on the human body. These peptides are integral in studies targeting the enhancement of natural growth hormone levels, which can impact lean muscle development, fat metabolism, and overall vitality. Researchers investigate the peptides' interactions with muscle and fat tissues, focusing on protein synthesis and cellular regeneration processes., HGH peptides facilitate research into anti-aging, recovery, and hormonal optimization, providing insights into potential therapeutic applications.

Is growth hormone banned in sport?

Yes, at all times, in and out of competition, under Section S2 of the World Anti-Doping Agency Prohibited List. Detection methods are established and used at major competitions. Anyone subject to anti-doping testing should treat this product as disqualifying.

How does HGH compare to IGF-1 LR3?

They sit at different points on the same axis. Somatropin binds the growth hormone receptor, and one of the main consequences is that the liver produces IGF-1. IGF-1 then acts on its own separate receptor. So growth hormone acts upstream and much of its activity is mediated by IGF-1 downstream. IGF-1 LR3 is a modified form of IGF-1 that acts on the IGF-1 receptor directly.

Buy GLP-1 Peptides: Research Grade & Lab Tested

GLP-1 stands for glucagon-like peptide-1. It’s a hormone the gut releases after a meal, cut from a larger precursor protein called proglucagon by cells in the intestinal lining. The active form is about 30 amino acids long. It was identified in the 1980s, and the work to characterize it involved groups led by Joel Habener, Svetlana Mojsov and Daniel Drucker.

Native GLP-1 doesn’t last long in the bloodstream. An enzyme called DPP-4 clips it within a couple of minutes, which is why it’s hard to study directly and why so much research has gone into longer-lasting molecules that act on the same receptor. One early lead came from an unlikely place: a peptide in the venom of the Gila monster that turned out to activate the GLP-1 receptor and resist DPP-4. The GLP-1 receptor is now one of the most studied targets in metabolic research.

What GLP-1 Is and How It Works

The Hormone

GLP-1 is glucagon-like peptide-1, a 30-residue hormone released by L-cells in the lining of the small intestine and colon. It's cut from a larger precursor protein, proglucagon, and appears in the bloodstream within minutes of eating. GLP-1 Peptides mimic these hormone in different animal bodies.

The Receptor

The GLP-1 receptor, written GLP-1R, is a class B G protein-coupled receptor. It signals mainly through Gs, which raises cyclic AMP inside the cell. The receptor is found in the pancreas, the stomach and intestine, the heart and several regions of the brain.

The Two-Minute Problem

Native GLP-1 is broken down within about two minutes by dipeptidyl peptidase-4, or DPP-4, an enzyme that clips two residues off its front end. That short life is the central problem in GLP-1 research, and most work on this receptor is really work on getting past it.

An Unusual Origin Story

Interest in this receptor grew after a peptide in Gila monster venom was found to activate it while resisting DPP-4. That finding, published in the 1990s, opened the field. The GLP-1 receptor has been a major focus of metabolic and endocrine research ever since.

Somatropin & Related Compounds

Human growth hormone is a protein hormone made by the pituitary gland. Somatropin is the same protein produced recombinantly: the human gene is inserted into cultured cells, usually bacteria, which then make the protein in quantity.

It is far larger than the short peptides elsewhere in the catalog, at 191 amino acids, and it is folded into a defined shape that it needs to keep. Research uses it to study growth hormone receptor signaling and the downstream production of IGF-1 in cell and animal models.

Somatropin is supplied here as research-grade material in 12 IU, 24 IU, 30 IU and 50 IU vials, all of the same recombinant protein. It arrives as a lyophilized powder in a sealed vial and is reconstituted with bacteriostatic water before laboratory use. Because it is a folded protein rather than a short peptide, it is more sensitive to temperature and handling than most compounds in the catalog, and cold storage from the moment it arrives matters, as does gentle handling during reconstitution. Growth hormone secretagogues such as tesamorelin, CJC-1295 and ipamorelin are a separate class with their own category, as is hCG. Every batch is tested by an independent laboratory for identity and purity, and the certificate of analysis is available for the lot you receive.

Prices are listed per vial on each product page and updated as stock moves. Delivery is within Costa Rica only and usually takes two to four business days, with free shipping on orders above $200 and bulk pricing on five or more vials of the same product. Our team can confirm availability, vial size and the expected delivery window before you order, and can send the certificate of analysis for a specific lot on request. The certificate states the IU content of the lot.

About Somatropin

Structure

A single chain of 191 amino acids with two internal disulfide bridges, folded into a bundle of four helices, with a molecular weight of about 22 kilodaltons. That makes it far larger than the short peptides elsewhere in the catalog. Its size and folded structure are the reason it behaves differently in storage and handling, and why protein stability is a research topic in its own right.

Receptor Signaling

Growth hormone acts on the growth hormone receptor, which sits on the surface of many cell types. One hormone molecule binds two receptor units at once, and that pairing starts a signaling chain inside the cell through the JAK2 and STAT5 pathway. A large share of laboratory research on somatropin focuses on this binding step and the signals that follow it.

IGF-1 as a Readout

One of the most measured downstream outputs of growth hormone signalling is IGF-1, a separate hormone made largely in the liver. Many studies track IGF-1 levels in animal models or cell systems as a readout of growth hormone receptor activity, rather than measuring the receptor directly. Its levels are also easier to measure than the growth hormone signal itself. IGF-1 analogues are a separate compound class with their own category in the catalog.

Reading the Research

Much of the published work on growth hormone involves the natural hormone, or studies carried out under clinical supervision, and results from those settings do not transfer to research material. Laboratory findings in cells and animal models describe how a signaling system works. They are not evidence of any effect in a person, and nothing on this page is supplied for human use.

Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

These are the questions researchers ask most often about somatropin. Because it is a folded protein rather than a short peptide, several of the answers differ from the other categories in our catalog.

What are HGH (Human Growth Hormone) Peptides?

HGH peptides or Somatropin is recombinant human growth hormone: a 191-amino-acid protein with the same sequence as the growth hormone made by the pituitary gland, produced by inserting the human gene into cultured cells. It is supplied here in vials labelled in international units, from 12 IU to 50 IU. Because it is a protein rather than a short peptide, it is more sensitive to storage and handling. Growth hormone secretagogues and IGF-1 analogues are separate classes with their own categories. Supplied for laboratory research use only.

How Do HGH (Human Growth Hormone) Peptides Work?

In research models, somatropin binds the growth hormone receptor on the cell surface. One hormone molecule engages two receptor units, which activates the JAK2 and STAT5 signaling pathway inside the cell. One of the best-studied downstream results is production of IGF-1, largely in the liver. Growth hormone secretagogues such as tesamorelin and CJC-1295 work differently: they act on the pituitary gland rather than on the receptor. These descriptions come from cell and animal research and establish no use outside the laboratory.

How are HGH (Human Growth Hormone) Peptides Typically Stored and Handled?

Somatropin ships as a lyophilized powder and should be stored refrigerated at 2 to 8 degrees Celsius from the moment it arrives, away from light and moisture. As a folded protein, it is more sensitive to heat and to physical agitation than a short peptide. Keep the vial sealed until reconstitution. Bacteriostatic water is the usual reconstitution fluid, and our vials hold 3 ml, so reconstitution volumes stay within that. Add the water slowly down the inside wall of the vial and swirl gently rather than shaking, since shaking can damage the protein. Once reconstituted, keep it refrigerated, do not freeze it, and use it within the window the protocol sets.

What are the Common Research Applications of HGH (Human Growth Hormone) Peptides?

Published laboratory work on somatropin falls into a few areas. Receptor studies measure how the hormone binds the growth hormone receptor and activates signaling inside the cell. Downstream studies track IGF-1 and other markers in animal models. Structural and stability studies look at how the protein folds, and how storage and handling conditions affect aggregation. Comparative studies set somatropin alongside growth hormone secretagogues, which reach the same system by a different route. Results from cell and animal models describe signaling, not effects in a person.

When Can I Expect My HGH (Human Growth Hormone) Delivery?

Orders are typically delivered within 2–4 business days from the date the order is placed. Delivery is within Costa Rica only. Timing can vary with carrier schedules, the delivery province and order processing. We confirm stock and the expected delivery window with you before an order is finalized.

Buy Metabolic & GLP-1 Compounds: Research Grade & Lab Tested

This category holds both peptides and non-peptide compounds. Semaglutide and tirzepatide are synthetic incretin peptides: semaglutide acts on the GLP-1 receptor, and tirzepatide acts on both the GIP and GLP-1 receptors. 5-amino-1MQ and AICAR are small molecules, not peptides, studied for their effects on enzymes that control cell metabolism. The lipotropic blend is a multi-ingredient solution rather than a peptide, so check its product page and certificate for the ingredient list. The peptides and small molecules ship as a lyophilized powder in a sealed vial and are reconstituted with bacteriostatic water before laboratory use.

Every batch is tested by an independent laboratory for identity and purity, and the certificate of analysis is available for the lot you receive. Prices are listed per vial on each product page. Delivery is within Costa Rica only and usually takes two to four business days, with free shipping on orders above $200 and bulk pricing on five or more vials of the same product. Our team can confirm availability, vial size and the expected delivery window before you order, and can send the certificate for a specific lot on request.

About the Compounds in This Category

Semaglutide

Semaglutide is a modified form of GLP-1, the gut hormone released after eating. Two amino acid swaps and an attached fatty-acid chain let it bind albumin in the blood, so it lasts about a week rather than minutes. Nearly all of its human data comes from clinical trials of licensed medicines.

Tirzepatide

Tirzepatide is a 39-amino-acid peptide built on the sequence of GIP, a second incretin hormone. It activates both the GIP and GLP-1 receptors, and a fatty-acid chain gives it a half-life of about five days. As with semaglutide, its human data comes from trials of licensed medicines.

5-Amino-1MQ and AICAR

Neither 5-amino-1MQ nor AICAR is a peptide. 5-amino-1MQ is a small molecule that blocks NNMT, an enzyme active in fat tissue, and its published work is in cultured fat cells and mice. AICAR activates AMPK, the cell's energy sensor, and is a common laboratory tool.

Reading the Research

Results from clinical trials of licensed medicines do not transfer to research material. For the small molecules, findings come from cells and mice. None of this is evidence of any effect in a person, and nothing in this category is supplied for human use.
